# Cooling Fans Constantly Run: Diagnosing Electrical Logic vs. Mechanical Failure

When a vehicle's cooling fans run continuously regardless of engine temperature, it is rarely just an annoyance; it is a symptom of a broken feedback loop between the sensor and the control logic. In your specific case with the 1995 Pontiac Grand Am, you've already ruled out the most common mechanical culprits: coolant leaks and low fluid levels. Since the system isn't losing inventory or overheating due to blockage, we can focus entirely on the electrical architecture that dictates fan behavior.

The primary function of these fans is not merely "running cooler" as a passive benefit, but actively managing thermal spikes during high-load events like towing, climbing hills, or idling in traffic. When they run constantly, you are forcing the radiator to work when it doesn't need to. This leads to unnecessary electrical load, draining your battery and straining the alternator, which can prematurely degrade these components. More critically, constant airflow prevents the engine from reaching its optimal operating temperature too quickly during cold starts. Modern engines rely on precise thermal ranges for catalytic converter efficiency and fuel mixture optimization; keeping the head gasket or thermostat in a sub-optimal state can reduce fuel economy and increase emissions over time.

To diagnose this, you must treat the cooling system as an embedded control system rather than a simple mechanical device. The flow of logic typically follows this path: Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor → Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or Fan Control Relay → Cooling Fans.

The ECT sensor acts as the input variable. It sends a voltage signal to the PCM that correlates directly with coolant temperature. If this sensor fails and reports a value of 105°C (221°F) when the actual coolant is at 90°C, the PCM believes an overheat condition exists and engages the fans immediately. This is the most common failure mode in vehicles of this era. You should verify the resistance of your ECT sensor against manufacturer specifications using a multimeter while monitoring live data if possible.

Next, consider the fan control relay or the dedicated fan controller module. In many GM vehicles from this period, there is a dual-fan circuit where one fan runs at low speed for normal operation and both run at high speed during an overheat event. If a fuse blows in the primary circuit, the PCM may default to running all fans continuously as a fail-safe strategy. Conversely, if the relay itself has internal shorts or sticking contacts, it will remain closed regardless of the signal from the PCM.

Another potential issue lies within the PCM logic itself, though this is less common than sensor failure. If the PCM detects an open circuit in the fan wiring due to corrosion or rodent damage, it may interpret this as "fans not working" and force them on continuously to prevent overheating, a phenomenon known as a default-safe state.

If you are comfortable with automotive diagnostics, use a scan tool to check for stored trouble codes related to the ECT sensor or fan circuits. Look specifically for codes indicating an implausible signal range. If no codes are present but fans still run, disconnect the temperature sender connector and observe the behavior; if fans stop running when the circuit is open (or depending on the specific vehicle logic), the fault lies with the PCM interpreting a missing input incorrectly.

Finally, while this issue is mechanical-electrical in nature, the principle of monitoring system health applies broadly to embedded systems development. Just as you must validate sensor inputs against physical reality to prevent runaway states in software, ensuring your hardware sensors match expected ranges prevents cascading failures in vehicle control units.
